title: Check if a number is prime (no factors other than 1 and itself: loop from 2 to sqrt(n)).
shortTitle: Check if a Number is Prime
keyPoints: A prime has exactly two divisors: one and itself; numbers below two are not prime by definition.
Testing divisors only up to the square root of N reduces the cost from O(n) to O(sqrt(n)) because divisors come in pairs.
Write the loop bound as i * i <= n to avoid computing a floating-point square root and its rounding errors.
Two is the only even prime; after checking two, testing only odd divisors roughly halves the iterations.
For very large primes used in cryptography, trial division is too slow and probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin are used.
Overflow caution: for N near Integer.MAX_VALUE, i * i can overflow; use long or compare i <= n / i instead.

s1_definition.oneliner: A prime has exactly two divisors, one and itself, and you only need to test divisors up to its square root.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Prime number** – an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.
- **Square-root optimization** – divisors come in pairs multiplying to N, so if no divisor exists up to sqrt(N), none exists at all.
- **Loop bound** – `i * i <= n` avoids a floating-point `Math.sqrt` and keeps the test in integers.
- **Even shortcut** – two is the only even prime; after checking two, loop only over odd candidates starting at three.
- **Complexity** – O(sqrt(n)) time, O(1) space for the trial-division approach.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India generating special indivisible token numbers for secure transactions. A token is valid only if it cannot be split evenly into smaller equal groups. Checking a token is like trying to divide a pile of coins into equal stacks of two, three, four, and so on. If no stack size up to the square root divides the pile evenly, the pile is indivisible, that is, prime.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Input: n
    │
    ▼
  n < 2? ──Yes──→ return false
    │ No
    ▼
  n == 2? ──Yes──→ return true
    │ No
    ▼
  n % 2 == 0? ──Yes──→ return false
    │ No
    ▼
  i = 3
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  i * i <= n?     │──No──→ return true (prime)
  │                  │
  │  Yes             │
  │    ▼             │
  │  n % i == 0?     │──Yes──→ return false (composite)
  │    │ No          │
  │    ▼             │
  │  i = i + 2       │
  │    └─────────────┘
  └──────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A prime number is an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are one and itself. The naive way to test primality is to try dividing by every number from two up to N minus one, but the key optimization is to stop at the square root of N. Divisors come in pairs that multiply to N, and in every pair one member is at most the square root, so if no divisor exists up to the square root there is none at all. That drops the work from linear to square-root time.

In code, handle the small cases first: numbers below two are not prime, two is the only even prime, and any other even number is immediately rejected. Then loop over odd divisors only, starting at three, which roughly halves the work. Write the loop bound as `i * i <= n` to avoid a floating-point square root, or `i <= n / i` for overflow safety near the integer limit.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, this validated special secure reference tokens that had to be prime for an indivisibility property. Because tokens were validated at high volume, the square-root optimization kept the issuing service fast. For a number like 7919, only about 44 checks were needed instead of nearly 8000.

The senior-level connection is to cryptography. Trial division handles moderate numbers, but the enormous primes in RSA key generation are far too large for it, so there probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin decide primality quickly with negligible error. A humble loop that checks divisors up to a square root is the same idea that, scaled up with smarter algorithms, protects real financial transactions.

Remember one sentence: test divisors only up to the square root because divisors come in pairs, and one of each pair is always at or below the square root.
